The New York Yankees are headed to the MLB playoffs! But they have a lot to figure out before they *likely* have to face the Boston Red Sox in a 3-game Wild Card series.
A big storyline surrounding the Yankees right now is what manager Aaron Boone will do with Anthony Volpe when Jazz Chisholm Jr. returns.
Since Jazz went to the IL (and Volpe was called up). Volpe has had his fair share of moments, and it begs the question: What will the Yankees' infield layout look like?
Yankees fans may hate to admit it, but with Volpe's previous playoff experience, it might be wise to give the kid a shot in October.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Predicted to 'Dump' Luis Gil Ahead of Playoffs
What Should the Yankees Do with Anthony Volpe?
Has Anthony Volpe done enough to remain on the Yankees roster? Should be play second or third base in the MLB playoffs in place of Jazz Chisholm Jr. or Ryan McMahon.
Over his last seven games, Anthony Volpe has a home run, two doubles, eight hits, 7 RBI, and scored three runs.
In all likelihood, Jazz still has his 2B spot when he returns, but Ryan McMahon?? That's another question.
Ryan McMahon’s career numbers with the Yankees:
🤮 171 G🤮 .212 AVG🤮 14 HR🤮 52 RBI🤮 .636 OPS
How would you grade McMahon’s time in pinstripes so far? pic.twitter.com/cVEPiw5FFF
— SleeperYankees (@SleeperYankees) September 17, 2026
What will Volpe's role be when Jazz comes back?
Second baseman Anthony Volpe (7 games).348 BA // 1 HR // 7 RBI // .400 OBP // .965 OPS#Yankees pic.twitter.com/cqwisk1tw7
— Fireside Yankees (@FiresideYankees) September 17, 2026
Ryan McMahon is batting .210 this season with 10 home runs, 34 RBI, and just 66 hits.
And half of his games are in a hitters' haven for lefties.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Get Strong Jasson Dominguez Message Ahead of MLB Playoffs
Anthony Volpe's 2026 Season at a Glance
While Anthony Volpe's 2026 stats don't light the world on fire, it's fair to note he hasn't been given an extended runway to make a major impact, as he's bounced between AAA and the Bigs frequently.
Across 63 games this season, Volpe is batting .253 (career-high) with 14 XBH, 26 RBI, and an OPS+ of 92 (also would be career-high).
He's cut down on some of the strikeouts, and is still working a decent amount of walks.
Yankees fans, let me know in the comments what you think Anthony Volpe's role should be with the team in October?
If it were me (and being clear, I'm not the GM!) I'd run Volpe out there in October at 3B. It gives the lineup right-left balance, and Anthony Volpe has at least shown a capability of putting the ball in play that Ryan McMahon hasn't.

Will Yankees' postseason first-timers prove to be ready for the moment?
This browser does not support the video element.
It’s common to think of the Yankees as a playoff-tested team. After all, this is the eighth time in nine years that they’ve made the postseason under manager Aaron Boone. And a quick look at some of their regulars shows a lineup that varies between a little bit and a wealth of October experience.
Player No. of Career Playoff Games
Cody Bellinger 76
Aaron Judge 65
Paul Goldschmidt 29
Trent Grisham 26
Jazz Chisholm, Jr. 24
Austin Wells 21
Anthony Volpe 21
Amed Rosario 11
Ryan McMahon 10
Ben Rice 6
José Caballero 3
But a few names are missing from that list: Shortstop George Lombard Jr., outfielder Spencer Jones, first baseman Luis García Jr. and outfielder Heliot Ramos. Those four have never played in the postseason, either with the Yankees or -- as is the case with García and Ramos -- with their previous teams.
Now, it’s possible that some of the injured veteran players -- Grisham and Chisholm, specifically -- could return to the lineup and send some of those new faces to the bench or off the playoff roster entirely. But it’s safe to say the Yankees are going to be counting on at least a few playoff newbies next month in their quest to win their first World Series since 2009.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said his youngsters and playoff newcomers have another advantage over players who are coming of age in other markets.
“You play for the Yankees, you play in New York,” he said, “it has a way of getting you ready for the postseason.”
This browser does not support the video element.
This has been something of a transitional year in the Major Leagues. Check out the first round of the 2023 Draft if you want proof. No fewer than 19 of the 37 first-round and sandwich picks have debuted, and many of them are already impact players with their teams.
“Players are getting to the big leagues at a very quick pace now and at a young age,” said Tigers manager A.J. Hinch, who has welcomed No. 3 pick Max Clark and AL Rookie of the Year favorite Kevin McGonigle to Detroit this year. “I don't think they're as wowed by the big steps that they're taking.”
For the Yankees, that class includes Lombard, who has acclimated nicely since being called up in early August. And Jones was recently lauded by none other than Aaron Judge, who said the rookie outfielder has “really evolved every single time he got called up, gotten a little bit better and a little bit better.”
Of course, there will be hiccups along the way. On Wednesday, Jones went 0-for-6 with five strikeouts and committed an error when he dropped a fly ball in center field. And Lombard couldn’t come up with a Victor Caratini grounder in the 13th that was ruled a single as the Twins walked off the Yankees.
But anyone who follows baseball knows bad days and bad plays are all part of the growth cycle of a Major League player. The key is to learn from them so you can limit them going forward. And all of it -- the good, the bad and the occasionally ugly -- helps prepare a young player for his first time playing in the crucible of October baseball.
The world is about to find out just how ready the young Yankees are. But Jones offered a bit of reassurance on Monday as he soaked up the post-clinch locker room celebration at Target Field.
“I think for us, we play better when the crowd gets louder,” he said. “I’m really excited for what’s to come.”

The New York Yankees have a lot of decisions to make for their postseason roster, from lineup construction to the outfield, rotation, and bullpen, to managing guys coming back from injury. Outside of the team's core foundation, almost nothing is settled, especially on the bubble.
One of those bubble spots entails the backup infielders behind a hopefully healthy Jazz Chisholm Jr., George Lombard Jr., and Ryan McMahon. As of right now, the Yankees have three of them on the roster: José Caballero, Amed Rosario, and Anthony Volpe. The former has a secured spot due to his speed and versatility, but the latter two aren't as secure.
It's entirely possible the Yankees carry 14 position players on the playoff roster, but that means somebody will have to go for Chisholm when he returns. It's widely believed the corresponding move will be to send Volpe back to the minors, but what if the Yankees went another direction?
Here's why Volpe should be the one who lands that final infield spot instead of Rosario, and how the Yankees can handle the roster math:
New look Anthony Volpe can provide value to Yankees
I am personally not drinking the Kool-Aid of any tangible offensive improvements for Volpe, at least in the short term. What he did at Triple-A was feast on inferior pitchers with his opposite-field approach, something that doesn't have a 1-to-1 conversion rate in the big leagues. That said, we know what he is throughout his career: a mediocre hitter with a career 84 OPS+ and an 89 OPS+ this season in 62 games entering Wednesday.
That said, the ability to hit is maybe the least important aspect for a bench player, particularly one on a team that will have pinch-hitting options on both sides of the plate but needs defenders to replace them.
Volpe was not a fit for this roster when he only played shortstop, something that he would no longer get a chance to do with Lombard entrenched at the position. Upon his demotion to Triple-A, he got experience at second and third base, with the former being the position he's played almost every day since he was recalled after Chisholm's injury. Early returns are positive there.
At this point, we can directly compare Volpe to Rosario, who has also predominantly played second and third base when he has played. While offense is likely not on the 25-year-old's side, defense and baserunning certainly are. He's a vastly superior defender, posting a 3 DRS, 5 FRV, and 5 OAA at shortstop earlier this season.
Volpe is also a much more aggressive baserunner, recording 10 stolen bases and being one of baseball's best at stealing third base, an extremely critical skill to have in close playoff games.
And all of this assumes that Volpe's bat remains as bad as it's been throughout his career. But what if he did make positive adjustments? What if this new approach, coupled with his improved plate discipline from Opening Day, makes him playable, even as a platoon bat? He's already had a few clutch hits, as we saw in the Twins' series.
Amed Rosario's 2026 struggles make him expendable
The one thing that Rosario has on Volpe is his hitting ability, particularly against left-handed pitching, but we've gotten enough samples this season to determine whether a player's reputation actually backs up the results. For Rosario? It's not pretty.
A career .287 hitter against lefties, Rosario is down to just .200 with a .602 OPS against them in 151 plate appearances, something that goes beyond a small sample size. His strikeout rate against them at 21.1 percent is the highest it's been in a decade, while his quality of contact has similarly tanked, even if he's been very unlucky (.262 wOBA vs. .306 xwOBA). Compare this to Volpe, who's slashing a mediocre (but better) .253/.323/.373 against lefties this season, so is Rosario's best strength now a weakness?
He's had pretty hefty reverse splits this season, which completely goes against why he was signed. The Yankees have significantly better options on both sides of the ball against righties, so it doesn't help them at all. When you factor in his defensive shortcomings? He really seems like someone who should be on the chopping block.
Rosario is a guy who can play corner outfield and three infield positions, but plays none of them well. In just 303 innings this season at third base, he has -8 OAA and -7 FRV. He's also managed to be minor negatives in just 48 combined innings in left field, right field, and second base. On a rate basis, he's arguably the worst defender in baseball, something that would be muted if his bat was going (or if the DH spot was more accessible).
He's not a bad baserunner at all. In fact, he's one of the faster guys on the team in terms of sprint speed, but the few times he's on base this season, he's rarely in motion. He has just three stolen bases in the last two seasons and has been a net-negative baserunner according to Baseball Savant's Baserunning Runs metric due to a lack of aggressiveness in taking the extra base.
When your one strength isn't much of a strength anymore, and your usage on the roster is diminished, it has us asking how Volpe could help the team with its roster construction in the postseason.
How the roster shakes out
It wouldn't even be a major roster disruptor. Rosario is almost always the last guy on the bench because of how little the team trusts him defensively. If his bat was that much of an upgrade in a platoon situation, they'd make that trade, but it hasn't.
Come playoff time, I can see a world where the Yankees play Volpe at second or third base in place of McMahon or Chisholm against a left-handed pitcher to increase the at-bat quality without a massive defensive drop-off. It would also give them another pinch-running option they might need in late and close situations, as one of the best base stealers on the team.
I don't expect the Yankees to want to get rid of Rosario, though. He can be left off the playoff roster without a problem. But he can't be removed before then, which could cause an issue if Chisholm is likely to return before the postseason begins.
Therefore, a potential solution could be to send a pitcher down and play with an extra position player down the stretch, but the team is running out of players with options. Volpe could also go down just to fit puzzle pieces and return a few days later.
Ultimately, whatever the Yankees decide, it might not be the difference between a playoff series or even a playoff game, but margins are margins. This has not been a team that has won enough close games late, so giving yourself as much of an advantage in those situations is paramount.

The New York Yankees will have a decision to make when Jazz Chisholm Jr. is back from the injured list.
Anthony Volpe is up in Chisholm's place, but he is looking like a completely different hitter after a stint in Triple-A. He has made some changes and is hitting .348/.400/.565 with a home run, two doubles, four stolen bases and seven RBIs. Before he was optioned, he had a .240 batting average and a .646 OPS with one home run in 56 games.
When Chisholm is back, he will go back to starting every day. Even though it's a down year for him, he had really turned things around before his injury. Before his injury, Chisholm was slashing .313/.398/.835 and had 10 stolen bases since Aug. 9.
If Volpe stays hot, the Yankees cannot really afford to keep him out of the lineup. On the other hand, they cannot bench Chisholm, who was swinging it well and has been a starter all year. What can they do then? Well, the Brewers could leave Volpe at second base and play Chisholm at third base.
Ryan McMahon has not been great at third base, and if Chisholm is swinging the bat like he was for a month before his injury, he would easily be the best option there. He is not as strong a defender there, but the Yankees would be much better offensively without McMahon in the lineup.
Of course, this is dependent on Volpe staying hot and Chisholm picking up where he left off. If both of those don't happen, it becomes a situation where the Yankees need to pick one or the other, and it seems like Chisholm would get the nod.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — La primera mañana de Clarke Schmidtde vuelta en la plantilla de los Yankees empezó con una pequeña petición, tras más de 14 meses alejado del montículo de las Grandes Ligas. Quería un café, a ser posible un café con leche, antes de su tan esperado regreso el miércoles en el Target Field.
El lanzador diestro ya tenía la adrenalina a tope. Schmidt entró en el partido que los Yankees perdieron por 5-4 en la 13.ª entrada ante los Twins como primer relevo tras Carlos Rodón, tomando el relevo en la séptima entrada con Nueva York perdiendo por 2-0. Era su primera aparición en las Grandes Ligas desde el 3 de julio de 2025.
Schmidt consiguió dos outs, ponchó a dos y permitió dos sencillos flojos en 24 lanzamientos, 13 de ellos strikes. Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó las 95,8 mph. Brent Headrick dejó a ambos corredores heredados en base antes de que los Yankees empataran el partido en la novena entrada con un doble de dos carreras de Anthony Volpe.
Para Schmidt, esa entrada tuvo más importancia que una simple salida como relevo. Dijo que su regreso fue muy emotivo tras someterse a una segunda operación de Tommy John y a una rehabilitación llena de días monótonos lejos de la competición. Su padre, Dwight, piloto de Delta Air Lines, se reorganizó la agenda para estar en Minnesota.
«Se parece mucho a tu debut», dijo Schmidt. «Por suerte, ahora me siento un poco más a gusto, pero creo que las emociones eran parecidas y sentí la misma descarga de adrenalina».
Los Yankees también pudieron comprobar de inmediato las limitaciones de su papel actual. Schmidt está lanzando desde el bullpen porque no hubo tiempo suficiente para prepararlo como titular antes de que termine la temporada regular. No le gustó nada haber llegado a tres cuentas de tres bolas contra cuatro bateadores, aunque los golpes que recibió fueron débiles.
Esa salida demostró que su brazo está respondiendo. Para los Yankees, que están evaluando todas las opciones para el bullpen de la postemporada, las próximas salidas servirán para ver si Schmidt es capaz de controlar sus lanzamientos bajo mayor presión y recuperarse siguiendo el ritmo de un relevista en octubre.
Schmidt vuelve sin uno de sus lanzamientos estrella
Schmidt confirmó el jueves que ya no lanza su «sweeper», un lanzamiento que, según él, contribuyó a los problemas en el codo que le llevaron a someterse a una cirugía de Tommy John tras terminar la temporada de 2025.
Él y el departamento de pitcheo de los Yankees modificaron el agarre durante la temporada 2025 para conseguir un movimiento más horizontal. Schmidt empezó a usar esa versión el 6 de mayo contra San Diego. Más tarde comentó que ese agarre requería más presión y fuerza de giro. Un mes después, unas molestias en el antebrazo derecho complicaron su recuperación entre salidas.
«Creo que lo que más influyó fueron los cambios de empuñadura a mitad de temporada», dijo Schmidt en marzo. «Cuando cambias de empuñadura, empiezas a ejercer una tensión diferente en distintas zonas del antebrazo y cosas así».
La propuesta había funcionado, lo que complicaba la decisión de descartarla.
«Estaba consiguiendo muy buenos resultados con eso, así que es difícil decir: “Vale, dejemos de lanzarlo”», dijo Schmidt. «Era como un arma de doble filo».
Cuánto cuesta realmente perder al líbero
Los datos de Statcast de 2025 muestran que Schmidt lanzó el «sweeper» el 12,2 % de las veces. Los bateadores tuvieron un promedio de bateo de 0,125 contra él, con un wOBA de 0,188, y generó una tasa de strikes fallidos del 35,8 %.
Los Yankees no necesitan necesariamente un sustituto que lo iguale en todo. El slider de Schmidt dio mejores resultados en cuanto a valor de carrera en 2025. Los rivales batearon .061 contra él, con un wOBA de .139, y ese lanzamiento valió siete carreras, frente a la única del «sweeper».
Su uso de lanzamientos ya había bajado desde el 23,7 % registrado en 2024. El miércoles lanzó cinco tipos de lanzamientos: bola rápida de cuatro costuras, cutter, slider, sinker y curva de nudillos.
Esa combinación les da a los Yankees varias rangos de velocidad y perfiles de movimiento sin tener que volver al agarre que, según Schmidt, le causaba tensión en el brazo.
Los Yankees muestran serenidad, pero aún tienen que pulir la ejecución
A Aaron Boone le gustó cómo se las apañó Schmidt en un partido reñido tras una ausencia tan larga, aunque dos lanzamientos mal colocados acabaran en sencillos.
«Se le veía muy en forma y no parecía nada agobiado ni con prisas», dijo Boone. «Es un partido reñido, tu primer partido en más de un año, y seguro que hay algo de nerviosismo. Creo que lo ha gestionado bastante bien. Con suerte, a medida que vaya jugando, irá cogiendo un poco más de ritmo».
Schmidt también se enfrentó al ritmo poco habitual del papel de relevo. Empezó a calentar en la primera entrada, cuando Rodón tenía dificultades, y luego tuvo que sentarse y esperar hasta la séptima.
«Como suele pasar en el bullpen, me dieron un poco de caña en la primera entrada», dijo Schmidt riéndose. «Pensé que Carlos iba a salir, estaba emocionado y la adrenalina me subía por las nubes. Y luego tuve que volver a sentarme y calmarme un momento».
Las pruebas de octubre pasan de la recuperación al repertorio
Los Yankees han dado de alta a Schmidt tras cinco partidos de rehabilitación en las ligas menores, en los que cedió tres carreras en siete entradas, ponchó a 11 y concedió una base por bolas. No lanzará dos días seguidos, y Boone ha dicho que podría hacer más de tres outs dependiendo de cómo vaya la recuperación.
La temporada 2025 de Schmidt había ido muy bien antes de la lesión. Acumuló un balance de 4-4 con una efectividad de 3,32 en 14 salidas como titular, mantuvo a sus rivales en un promedio de bateo de 0,199 y encadenó una racha de 28 1/3 entradas sin encajar carreras en junio.
Ahora los Yankees están evaluando algo diferente. En su primera noche tras el regreso, mostró una velocidad de unos 90, dos strikeouts por swing y la compostura suficiente para afrontar un regreso lleno de adrenalina. El lanzamiento «sweeper» ya no está, y los Yankees necesitan ver si el resto del arsenal de Schmidt puede asumir la carga de trabajo que antes ayudaba a llevar ese lanzamiento.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario abajo.

Ryan McMahon's tenure with the New York Yankees hasn't gone as planned. He has certainly been a strong fielder at third base (though not as exceptional as he was sold), but his bat has been anemic by any metric. So much so that after going 0-for-6 with four strikeouts on Wednesday, he has officially joined similar territory as a number of infamous Yankees who underperformed during their time in pinstripes.
As pointed out by Jack Fungo on X, McMahon has a 80 wRC+ in 162 games since being acquired by the Yankees at the 2025 trade deadline. That is a lower mark than DJ LeMahieu's final season with the Yankees when he got released, Josh Donaldson's career in the Bronx, Joey Gallo's time with the Yankees, Isiah Kiner-Falefa's 2023 season and Anthony Volpe's 2025 season.
Ryan McMahon's Yankees company proves the DFA bells are tolling
This isn't great company to be in for McMahon. To put things in perspective, McMahon is 20 points below the league average of 100 for wRC+. On the season, McMahon has hit 10 home runs, has driven in 34 RBI and sports a .210/.275/.346 slash line with a .621 OPS.
McMahon had some solid offensive years with the Colorado Rockies in his career, but his home splits were always much better due to his numbers at Coors Field being inflated as a result of the high altitude. The writing appeared to be on the wall for McMahon before he switched cities.
But the Yankees traded for McMahon because they were desperate for a third baseman last year. They also landed Amed Rosario to platoon with McMahon at the hot corner. Neither has stepped up to claim the job on an everyday basis, though Rosario's bat has been markedly better lately (.348 average in his last seven sporadically placed games).
Should Rosario's hot streak continue into the end of the regular season, the Yankees find a way to utilize him at third base during the postseason. There's even a world where Jose Caballero slides to third, with Anthony Volpe available off the bench. McMahon will probably still get a roster spot, but they cannot play his bat regularly in the biggest games of the year. McMahon's bat creates a black hole in the Yankees' lineup, which they cannot afford to deploy in October.
If not for his defense, McMahon would've likely been designated for assignment by now. And given his historically poor offensive numbers, it seems like it could be headed that way with McMahonunder contract for another year at $16 million. The 31-year-old just has not worked out as a member of the Yankees, and his time in pinstripes should come to an end sooner rather than later.

Rodón se fue del partido con los Yankees perdiendo por 2-0. Anthony Volpe igualó el marcador con un doble de dos carreras en la novena entrada, y Nueva York se puso por delante tanto en la décima como en la undécima. Minnesota respondió en cada ocasión hasta que un sencillo de Víctor Caratini, como bateador suplente, puso fin al partido en la decimotercera entrada. Tommy Nance se llevó la victoria, mientras que John Schreiber se llevó la derrota.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 88-64. Tampa Bay ganó más tarde ese mismo miércoles, lo que deja a Nueva York a 4,5 partidos de los Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero las decisiones que tengan que tomar ahora sobre la rotación de lanzadores tendrán repercusiones en la clasificación de la división y en el orden de salida en octubre.
Los resultados de Rodón siguen siendo sólidos. El miércoles sumó su 25.ª salida consecutiva en la que ha cedido tres carreras limpias o menos, todo un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees. Además, ha encadenado dos salidas de calidad seguidas y ha logrado su quinta salida de calidad en 15 partidos, después de haber lanzado 6 1/3 entradas contra los Mets en su anterior salida.
Su carga de trabajo también ha ido por buen camino. Rodon lanzó 102 lanzamientos el miércoles, su mejor marca de la temporada, tras haber llegado a los 93 lanzamientos contra los Mets. Desde que volvió de la lista de lesionados a mediados de agosto, tiene una efectividad de 2,40, un WHIP de 0,93 y una relación de 31 ponches por cada 12 bases por bolas en 30 entradas.
Para los Yankees, sin embargo, la pregunta que surge tras la visita a Minnesota no es si Rodon podrá aguantar una salida. Es si podrá recuperar su potencia habitual lo suficientemente rápido, ahora que las alineaciones de octubre dejan menos margen para una puesta en marcha gradual.
El calendario deja a los Yankees poco tiempo para distinguir entre una fluctuación temporal y una tendencia que se repita.
Los primeros 55 lanzamientos cuentan una historia diferente
La preocupación se notó desde el principio en todo el repertorio de lanzamientos de Rodon, no solo en su bola rápida de cuatro costuras. La instantánea del seguimiento de lanzamientos adjunta a la salida mostraba que sus cinco lanzamientos estaban por debajo de su velocidad media de la temporada tras 55 lanzamientos.
Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó una media de 92,6 mph, frente a la media de la temporada de 94,4 mph, lo que supone una caída de 1,8 mph. Su slider bajó 1,4 mph, su cambio de velocidad 2,3 mph, su sinker 1,9 mph y su curva 1,1 mph.
Recurrió a la bola rápida de cuatro costuras en el 45 % de esos primeros 55 lanzamientos y al slider en el 29 %. Eso significa que casi tres cuartas partes de su repertorio inicial procedían de dos lanzamientos que estaban 1,8 mph y 1,4 mph por debajo de sus valores habituales de la temporada.
Eso hace que esa caída inicial sea más notable que el dato de una sola bola rápida. El cambio de velocidad fue el que mostró la mayor diferencia, mientras que ambos tipos de bola rápida estaban casi 2 mph por debajo de sus niveles anuales.
Pero Rodon no se quedó ahí. Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó una media de 92,3 mph en la primera entrada, 92,8 en la segunda y 92,4 en la tercera. En la cuarta, esa media subió a 94,9 mph, y más tarde lanzó varios lanzamientos por encima de las 95 mph.
Rodon necesitaba tiempo para soltarse un poco
Rodon habló después sobre su mal comienzo. La información disponible tras el partido no especificaba que esa rigidez se debiera a su codo. Describió cómo se sentía al principio, antes de que su velocidad mejorara a medida que avanzaba el partido.
Rodon dijo que empezó el partido un poco «tenso» antes de soltarse.
Esa formulación es importante por su historial médico de 2026. Rodon empezó la temporada en la lista de lesionados tras someterse a una operación durante la pretemporada para extirparle un espolón óseo del codo izquierdo. Más tarde volvió a la lista de lesionados por una inflamación en el codo izquierdo y se reincorporó el 18 de agosto tras un periodo de rehabilitación.
No se determinó que esa molestia fuera un problema en el codo, y no se informó de ninguna nueva lesión de Rodon tras el partido. Aun así, los Yankees tendrán motivos para estar atentos a la rapidez con la que recupere su velocidad en su próxima salida, tras una temporada acortada por las lesiones.
Los buenos resultados están ocultando una carga de trabajo más intensa
La eficacia de Rodón se ha mantenido intacta, aunque la forma de llegar a las seis entradas haya cambiado. Contra los Mets, el 11 de septiembre, necesitó 93 lanzamientos para completar 6 1/3 entradas, concedió una base por bolas y ponchó a ocho. Cinco días después, necesitó 102 lanzamientos para completar seis entradas, con tres bases por bolas y cinco ponches.
De los 102 lanzamientos del miércoles, solo 59 fueron strikes, algo menos del 58 %. Aun así, limitó a Minnesota a cuatro hits y dos carreras, pero el mayor número de corredores en base y los conteos más ajustados hicieron que esta salida le costara más esfuerzo que su anterior salida.
Teniendo en cuenta sus estadísticas de la temporada hasta el miércoles y su actuación final contra Minnesota, Rodon tiene ahora una ERA de aproximadamente 2,95 en 76 1/3 entradas repartidas en 15 salidas como titular. Los Yankees han contado con él para evitar que el rival anote cuando ha estado disponible.
La salida de los Rays sube el listón
Se espera que la próxima salida de Rodón sea durante la serie de cuatro partidos en casa de los Yankeescontra Tampa Bay, que empieza el martes con una doble jornada dividida en el Yankee Stadium. Nueva York lleva un balance de 3-6 contra los Rays esta temporada.
Ese partido podría ser su última salida como titular en la temporada regular. Además, les da a los Yankees la oportunidad de comprobar directamente si la caída en la velocidad de los lanzamientos del miércoles fue algo puntual o algo que le va a acompañar a Rodon en la postemporada.
Los Yankees obtendrán su siguiente dato cuando le toque lanzar a Rodon contra Tampa Bay, con la lucha por el título de división y la rotación de la postemporada aún en juego.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe is four games into his new role as a big-league second baseman after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Volpe hasn't committed an error yet, and while the sample is tiny, the eye test feels so right. Volpe just looks comfortable out there.
His Jeter-esque jump throw on Sunday (from second base, but still!) was such a rewarding watch for Yankees fans who have experienced the dreadful lows of Volpe's up-and-down season and career. It looked and felt so much more iconic than it was.
It didn't take long for Anthony Volpe to learn second base for the Yankees
Volpe looking smooth at second is a bittersweet reality for Yankees fans, especially those with a quick trigger to criticize the team's development and roster decisions. On one hand, New York's decision to send Volpe down to the minors and learn second base this season has ... worked! On the other hand, this exact plan should have been put into motion a long time ago.
It's kind of like turning in your book report a month late in middle school. The teacher is like, "Well, thanks ... but I just remembered again that you never handed this in." You might've been better off just taking the zero and acing the next one.
If Volpe keeps acing second base — and sustains this level of defense into 2027 and beyond alongside George Lombard Jr. — the Yankees will have salvaged Volpe's career and somewhat made up for their entire mishandling of his development.
Then again, should the Yankees really get any credit for salvaging anything here, especially since it was the organization itself that contributed to this mess? Even now, it took an injury to Chisholm (not his horrid season and Volpe's red-hot bat in the minors) to give Volpe another opportunity. This decision was made for the Yankees, not by them. And it came way, way too late. On second thought, they don't get any credit here.
Anthony Volpe as a second-base solution should have been obvious to the Yankees years ago
Any player evaluator of worth should have been able to look at Volpe and surmise that a move from shortstop to second base made sense. Volpe won a Gold Glove as a rookie shortstop in 2023, but his range, arm, and consistency declined after that. Isn't that pretty much the precise recipe for a move from short to second, if you had to literally write the script?
The Yankees' problem with Volpe over the years, as has been acknowledged ad nauseam, is that they made "New York Yankees starting shortstop" Volpe's identity (rather than his job) and hugged that identity too tightly. It became a stranglehold that suffocated Volpe and had Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman at their most delusional in interviews, which is saying a lot.
The funny thing is that Volpe's never been against changing positions. He said unironically that he'd play catcher. It was Boone and Cashman who were stubborn, and they never actually lessened their grip on this situation. George Lombard Jr. undid that grip for them, and then Chisholm went down.
To the non-Yankee fan, the Yankees might look smart for putting Volpe at second base. But for the die-hards, this decision — and Volpe's good performance at second so far — hurts as much as it excites. At least for now.

The New York Yankees are focused on the postseason and are looking to end their World Series drought, which has lasted over 15 years. Nonetheless, there are takes and opinions to help the team improve this upcoming offseason.
It's been a rollercoaster 2026 MLB season for Anthony Volpe, who was optioned to Triple-A in August and then recalled in September. Still, it might be in the 25-year-old's best interest to get a fresh start elsewhere.
Christopher Kline of FanSided floated a trade idea that would send Volpe along with LHP Brent Headrick and LHP Kyle Carr to the St. Louis Cardinals for 24-year-old shortstop Masyn Winn.
"The Yankees' lack of fundamental soundness on the defensive end has bitten them in the you-know-what all season, just like it did last year," Kline wrote in a Sept. 16 article. "The hope was that top prospect George Lombard Jr. could steady the ship at shortstop, but he has stacked up errors left and right.
"It's too early to write off the 21-year-old long term, but he could serve more comfortably at third or second — which is notable, since Jazz Chisholm Jr. is about to [be a free agent]. Winn immediately alleviates a ton of defensive issues for the Yankees, while his weaker bat would be well-protected in the American League's most potent lineup."
Yankees Have Assets to Trade for Cardinals' Masyn Winn
Since being recalled on Sept. 9, Volpe has performed well. Entering Sept. 17, Volpe has been batting .348 with eight hits, a home run, seven RBIs, and three runs scored in seven games, per StatMuse. Meanwhile, Kline believes Volpe can benefit from a move, while the Yankees would upgrade their defense in the infield with Winn.
"New York has the resources to one day pay Winn his worth, too, although three additional years of club control means those conversations are in the distant future," Kline added in his article. "This move allows St. Louis to bump Wetherholt to shortstop and plug in former top prospect Anthony Volpe at second base, where he has looked much more solid of late in New York."
Anthony Volpe Would Benefit From a Move Out of New York
As for what Winn can bring to the plate, entering Sept. 17, he has a batting average of .237 with 107 hits, five homers, 54 RBIs, and 52 runs scored in 129 games this season, per StatMuse.
Moreover, Volpe would benefit from a move to the Cardinals, where Kline believes the team could move him to second base, where he might thrive. The two bullpen arms would bolster St. Louis' bullpen and still have a handful of years under control to help in their rebuild.
"Volpe is a former Gold Glove shortstop whose defensive profile is very much salvageable, especially at a less demanding position," Kline noted in his article. "He's also a hitter with more upside right now, with the potential to add real pop to the back half of St. Louis' lineup.
"The Cardinals also add high-leverage reliever Brent Headrick, with a 1.94 ERA and five years of club control, and 24-year-old southpaw Kyle Carr, a Triple-A arm who profiles as a potential back-end starter with plus command."

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Anthony Volpe bateó con tanta fuerza que perdió el equilibrio, convencido de que la pelota se había ido fuera. En cambio, rebotó contra el muro alto del centro-derecha, un doble de dos carreras que igualó el marcador para los Yankees con dos outs en la novena entrada. Durante un momento intenso y emocionante el miércoles, Nueva York parecía dispuesta a llevarse la barrida.
Lo que vino después fueron cuatro entradas más en las que el equipo llegaba hasta la puerta y se negaba a cruzarla. Los Yankees se pusieron por delante en la décima. Volvieron a hacerlo en la undécima. Llenaron las bases sin outs en la duodécima. Cada vez acababan con un empate o con una remontada desperdiciada.
Un viaje que debería haber acabado con una barrida acabó poniendo de manifiesto el único punto débil que un aspirante al título no puede permitirse arrastrar hasta octubre. No se trató de un colapso del bullpen ni de un rebote desafortunado. Fue la alineación de los Yankees la que no paraba de preparar la mesa, pero nunca se sentaba a comer.
La culpa final recayó en un novato que no se la merecía él solo.
Los Minnesota Twins vencieron a los Yankees por 5-4 en 13 entradas, poniendo fin a ese partido maratoniano con un sencillo de Victor Caratini en la primera base que rebotó en el montículo y se coló por debajo del guante de George Lombard Jr. en la segunda base. Con esta derrota, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-64, a cuatro partidos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en los playoffs, pero el título de la división y la exención de la primera ronda se les están escapando.
Una remontada que no llevó a ninguna parte
Nueva York había sumado cuatro hits en ocho entradas y perdía por 2-0, mientras que el lanzador diestro de los Twins, Zebby Matthews, había ponchado a ocho. Entonces llegó la novena entrada. Lombard conectó un sencillo, Paul Goldschmidt le siguió y el corredor suplente José Caballero preparó el terreno para Volpe.
Volpe impulsó las dos carreras, lo que le supuso al cerrador de los Twins, Yoendrys Gómez, su primer salvamento fallido del año y obligó a jugar entradas extras.
Ali Sánchez impulsó al corredor automático con un sencillo en la décima entrada, dando a los Yankees su primera ventaja. Luke Keaschall respondió con un sencillo que empató el partido ante David Bednar. Un fly de sacrificio de Caballero puso a Nueva York por delante en la undécima. Royce Lewis igualó el marcador. Dos ventajas, dos respuestas inmediatas.
La entrada que dará que hablar
La 12.ª es la entrada que los aficionados volverán a ver una y otra vez. Los Yankees llenaron las bases sin outs, la situación que debería haber sentenciado el partido. Pero no sacaron nada de ella.
Heliot Ramos, que bateaba en el turno de Aaron Judge, mandó una bola corta hacia el montículo. Travis Adams la convirtió en una doble jugada 1-2-3. Sánchez se fue con un strikeout, dejando a otros dos en base. Los Yankees acabaron con 7 de 30 con corredores en posición de anotar.
El juez se marcha y el ataque se queda con pocos jugadores
Judge se retiró en la sexta entrada por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha que empezó a notar en la primera entrada. Falló dos veces y no volvió al campo, solo siete partidos después de una ausencia de 99 días. Por eso Ramos estaba bateando en su lugar.
El entrenador Aaron Boone describió la noche como una oportunidad perdida, no como un partido robado, y sus palabras reflejaban la importancia del momento en el calendario.
«Obviamente, muchas cosas buenas, pero no las suficientes», dijo Boone. «Ha sido un golpe duro, claro, cuando tenías la oportunidad de barrer la serie y justo antes de un día de descanso. Pero tenemos que superarlo y prepararnos para enfrentarnos a un buen equipo de los Diamondbacks».
Al final del partido, Boone no se anduvo con rodeos con Lombard, pero tampoco lo machacó.
Boone reconoció que la bola de Caratini rebotó en el montículo, pero fue una jugada que Lombard «se espera que haga y sabemos que es capaz de hacer».
Rodón lo da todo en octubre, pero no saca nada a cambio
Carlos Rodón le dio a los Yankees el comienzo que necesita una rotación en la postemporada y vio cómo se esfumaba. El zurdo encajó dos carreras en seis entradas, ampliando su récord de la franquicia a 25 salidas consecutivas en las que ha encajado tres carreras o menos. Lanzó 102 lanzamientos, su máximo de la temporada, y bajó su promedio de carreras limpias a 2,95.
«Empecé un poco lento, un poco tenso», dijo Rodon. «Me fui soltando en las siguientes entradas, así que eso estuvo bien».
Clarke Schmidt hizo su tan esperado regreso en la séptima entrada, ponchando a dos antes de que Brent Headrick dejara a dos en base. El bullpen corrió una maratón que la alineación nunca supo recompensar.
Una primicia para el club que no se veía desde 1991
Este es el dato que pocos destacarán. Ha sido la primera derrota de los Yankees tras ir ganando varias veces en entradas extras desde el 5 de mayo de 1991, en Seattle, es decir, en un lapso de más de 34 años. También fue su octava derrota en la última entrada de la temporada, un récord de la franquicia, y ningún equipo de la MLB ha encajado más hits decisivos en la última entrada en 2026, según datos de Baseball Reference. Ningún equipo de los Yankees ha perdido nunca más partidos a domicilio en entradas extras en una sola temporada.
Lo curioso es que los equipos malos no acumulan cifras como estas. Un equipo mediocre pierde en nueve partidos. Solo un buen equipo es capaz de forzar una prórroga fuera de casa una y otra vez, y luego seguir perdiéndola.
Cómo queda la carrera por la División Este de la Liga Americana
Spencer Jones lanzó su propia advertencia, ponchándose cinco veces en una noche en la que se fue de 0 de 6, lo que demostró lo rápido que se castigan los swings fallidos cuando los márgenes se estrechan. En septiembre se lee de otra manera que en julio.
Los Yankees tienen el jueves libre antes de empezar una serie de fin de semana en Arizona, donde Gerrit Cole será el lanzador titular el viernes a las 21:40 h (hora del Este). No se espera que Judge tenga que hacerse más pruebas. Nueva York ha perdido terreno que quizá no recupere y le ha dado un respiro a los Rays.
Los Yankees saben cómo ganar los partidos intermedios. Una noche en la que solo tenían que ganar uno, no pudieron.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.

Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.

On Wednesday afternoon, the New York Yankees and Minnesota Twins are finishing their series at Target Field.
The Yankees have won each of the first two games, so they are looking to go for the sweep.
Anthony Volpe finished Saturday’s 8-1 victory with two hits, one walk and one stolen base.

Boone Makes Volpe Statement
In a recent interview with Jomboy Media’s Talkin’ Yanks, manager Aaron Boone was asked about Volpe (h/t Talkin’ Yanks).
The 25-year-old hit a grand slam in his first game back at the MLB level (on September 10).
Jomboy: “That was a cool day. It was cool to hear the fans back him, cool to hear his quotes. For me personally, just cool to see a new approach at the plate. Kind of drastically different in terms of a baseball swing. He’s stepping back. You in your quote, said he’s definitely grounding himself more on that back leg. His hands are in a new position. So I was wondering if you could peel back the curtain on how does that new approach happen? Is that minor league coaches? Is that Rowson sending down to the minor league coaches, or is that Volpe on his own?”
Boone: “I think it’s the hitting department, Jarret DeHart getting involved. I don’t think it’s anything drastically new. He’s been that at different times, it’s just getting consistent and getting into a good place down there. And to me, when he came back up, it just looked more grounded. I feel like he’s getting to stronger positions… There’s only been… four, five, six games, so he’s gotten some results, but I also feel like there’s been some swings where he’s just missed… A couple balls deep to right that I feel like he’s kind of on time for and getting into a strong position. I thought last night, coming off the bench, he put a good at-bat where he hits the ball well to left. So those are all good signs that he’s on some things, and he’s doing a good job with the whole field but not sacrificing authority in his swing. He’s getting a good swing off.”

Volpe is in the middle of his fourth season at the MLB level (all with New York).
He came into Wednesday batting .249 with 47 hits, two home runs, 24 RBIs, 23 runs and 10 stolen bases in 62 games.

Jones entered the game batting .259/.331/.452 with 10 home runs. His hitless afternoon dropped that line to .252/.323/.440, while his strikeout rate sits around 35 percent.
Twins starter Zebby Matthews held the Yankees to two hits across six scoreless innings while recording eight strikeouts. Carlos Rodon countered by allowing two runs on four hits across six innings for New York.

Captain Aaron Judge exited the New York Yankees' game against the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday with right-leg tightness.
Outfielder Heliot Ramos pinch hit for Judge during his spot in the sixth inning. Judge was 0-for-2 with a pair of strikeouts.
The Yankees did not initially provide any update the injury, leaving fans to speculate the worst for nearly an hour before YES' Meredith Markaovits reported the leg prognosis.
Judge missed 84 games with a stress fracture in his right rib, and the Yankees were one of the worst offensive teams in baseball in that span.
Judge returned Sept. 8 against the Colorado Rockies — he left that game early too — and hit his first home run since coming back from the injury in the Yankees' 8-3 win over the Twins that clinched a playoff berth Monday.
The Yankees captain got the day off Tuesday, and the Yankees are off Thursday before their three-game weekend series against the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Judge is slashing .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs through 66 games.
Aaron Judge Left Wednesday's Yankees Game in the Sixth Inning
YES Network cameras captured Judge appearing to grimace during a check swing in his final at-bat. He remained in the game, struck out again in the third inning to strand two runners then fielded Ben Ross' double off the wall in the fifth inning.
But all of Yankees Universe held its breath when Ramos stepped up to the plate in Judge's spot for the sixth inning, especially after YES Network analyst and Judge's former manager, Joe Girardi, said what Yankees fans were thinking.
"Something has to be up," Girardi said.
Ramos, whom the Yankees acquired from the San Francisco Giants before the trade deadline as insurance for Judge, struck out in his at-bat. He took over in right field in the bottom of the sixth inning.
The Yankees Can't Afford to Lose Aaron Judge
The Yankees were being shut out when Judge exited the game Wednesday, held in check by Twins starter Zebby Matthews.
But you can feel the sigh of relief from Yankees fans after Marakovits' reporting.
The Yankees offense was again beginning to find its footing with Judge back. They ranked tied for 26th in the majors in runs, 26th in slugging percentage (.386) and dead last in on-base percentage (.295) over the three-plus months Judge was out of the lineup.
Judge's postseason struggles are well-documented, but the Yankees really can't afford not to have him in their lineup when the calendar flips to October with any injury.
Aside from being a three-time American League MVP, Judge also balances out the Yankees' left-hand-heavy lineup, joining infielders Anthony Volpe and George Lombard Jr. as the only righties in their regular starting nine.
A second straight wild-card-round date with the Boston Red Sox, and their co-ace lefties Garrett Crochet and Payton Tolle, is looming. The Yankees are already likely to be without Giancarlo Stanton and not having Judge would be even more problematic.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS -- The first two games of this week’s series at Target Field couldn’t have gone much better for the Yankees. They won both handily, and on Monday Aaron Judge hit his first home run since returning from the IL on Sept. 8.
Judge, who sat out Tuesday’s game as a routine day off after playing six straight games, struck out in each of his first two at-bats against Twins starter Zebby Matthews on Wednesday. After the game, he said he felt a stiffness in his lower right leg in the first inning.
“I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch,” Judge said. “But kind of talking it over, I thought it'd be the right move to come out, so I don't cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepath.”
With an off-day scheduled for Thursday, the team will wait to issue any prognosis on the severity of the injury until after he’s received extensive treatment over the next 48 hours.
“We’re not going to speculate one way or the other. We’ll just see how he responds,” manager Aaron Boone said.
Judge, who said he didn’t anticipate getting testing done, said he couldn’t pinpoint any specific activity or movement that triggered the stiffness, but the feeling isn’t an unfamiliar one to him.
“I feel like you deal with this every Spring Training. You know, usually at the start of the season once you start ramping up again, things pop up, and that's where we've been,” Judge said. “Thankfully, this whole time coming back, nothing's really nagged us. So hopefully it's just one little thing and then we're back out there soon.”
It would be a huge blow to the team to lose Judge after just getting him back into the lineup for the first time in three months. But at the same time, professional athletes and their coaches have to keep an eye on the big picture, and one Wednesday afternoon game against the Twins in mid-September pales in importance compared to upcoming series against the Diamondbacks, Rays and Orioles, plus whatever postseason action the team might see.
That’s especially true when that four-game series against Tampa Bay starting Tuesday could still determine the AL East champions -- and potentially a first-round bye in the postseason.
“Obviously he’s a key figure of what we do,” Boone said. “Hopefully we get it treated and knock it out and be a factor at some point.”
Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for Judge and also struck out against Matthews, who fanned eight in six scoreless innings. Ramos would likely fill in for Judge in right field during any absence he might incur.
The Yankees certainly could have used Judge’s bat in the lineup as they traded blows with the Twins in extra innings, after Anthony Volpe smacked a game-tying double off the wall in the top of the ninth with his club down to its final out.
In the 12th, the Yanks squandered an opportunity with the bases loaded and nobody out, as Ramos grounded into a double play, with Volpe thrown out at home plate. Ali Sánchez then struck out to end the threat, before Twins pinch-hitter Victor Caratini delivered a walk-off single up the middle in the 13th.

New York Yankees fans may not like it, but Anthony Volpe is answering a big offseason question for the team.
It was just six weeks ago that New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe was a pariah in the Bronx. He was demoted to Triple-A to clear room for George Lombard Jr. at shortstop, and there was no clear path for him back to the major leagues.
Then, last week, the Yankees placed Jazz Chisholm on the 10-day injured list due to a thumb injury, and suddenly, an avenue opened for Volpe.
New York recalled the 25-year-old from the minor leagues and put him at second base, and the early returns have been impressive.
Since rejoining the big-league club, Volpe has gone 8-for-22 with a grand slam, and on Wednesday afternoon against the Minnesota Twins, he smacked a game-tying two-run double off the wall in the ninth inning.
Why? Because Chisholm is hitting free agency in November, and New York seems very unlikely to re-sign him.
Yes, names like Luis Arraez and Brandon Lowe will be available, and they would obviously represent massive upgrades, particularly offensively. But will the Yankees want to shell out the cash necessary to land either one of them?
Volpe makes sense for New York as a Chisholm replacement.
Is it the way New York initially hoped? No. Volpe was initially supposed to be the Yankees' shortstop of the future, and when he won a Gold Glove and smashed 21 home runs during his rookie campaign in 2023, he appeared to be on quite a trajectory.
His second and third seasons, however, were massively disappointing, which, combined with a 2025 shoulder injury that required offseason surgery, has resulted in the up-and-down adventure we have seen this year.
But the Yankees no longer operate like the Evil Empire of the George Steinbrenner years. If they can effectively cut costs, they will, and that will be even more applicable if and when a salary cap is instituted this winter.
Volpe has been playing very well since getting back into the big leagues, and his walk rate on the campaign overall (11.2 percent) has represented a major improvement.
Don't think New York hasn't taken notice.

It's been a nice start to the week in the Yankees' home-away-from-home. On Monday night, they clinched a postseason berth with a 7-3 win against the Twins. On Tuesday evening, they fielded the proverbial "hangover lineup" of sorts and still cruised to an 8-1 victory behind a strong start from Max Fried and plenty of strong performances at the plate.
On today's getaway day game in Minneapolis, Carlos Rodón leads the Yankees' effort for a sweep. His most recent start against the Mets was perhaps the best of his season, as he held down the crosstown rivals for one run in 6.1 innings—with eight strikeouts to just one walk. For Rodón, who has for various reasons not pitched deep into games as routinely as he did in 2025, a second straight start of six or more innings would be an excellent sign as he prepares for the postseason.
The Twins, now 4-9 in September, will look to young righty Zebby Matthews, who has turned in an uneven campaign on the hill this season. His past three starts have been illustrative of the step-forward-step-back tendency which has tormented many a young hurler. On August 30th, he twirled an absolute gem, pitching into the ninth inning against the rival White Sox with just one run allowed in a win. His next appearance, also against Chicago, was a far more pedestrian five-inning, four-run effort. Then last time out, he failed to escape the third inning in Detroit—walking four batters and surrendering five runs to hit the showers early.
While the Yankees rested a few of their starters for last night's contest, including Aaron Judge, it didn't prevent them from running up the score. Today, Judge returns to the lineup card, hitting third behind DH Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, who led the way with three hits and a homer last night. Cleanup hitter Luis García Jr., Spencer Jones, and George Lombard Jr. will make up the middle of the order, with Ryan McMahon, Austin Wells, and second baseman Anthony Volpe (it's still weird to say that) pulling up the rear.

There’s no doubt that the youngster has untapped potential to become a star, but after more than 30 games, his inexperience is starting to really show. Even as the team clinched another playoff berth, Lombard Jr. has displayed a concerning lack of polish that may end up costing the Yankees dearly in October.
This isn’t meant to dunk on the young shortstop. He’s done about as well as you’d expect a 21-year-old to play considering the situation. Even seasoned veterans have struggled to handle the bright spotlight in the Bronx, especially anyone who has attempted to start at shortstop. But just from the eye test, Lombard Jr. has been prone to making mental mistakes, especially when it comes to speeding up his internal clock on defense.
During the Yankees’ 8-3 win over the Minnesota Twins on Sept. 14, Lombard Jr. fielded a throw from second baseman Anthony Volpe in the bottom of the ninth. What should have been a simple force out instead led to both runners being called safe after Lombard Jr. rushed the play in an attempt to try and turn two. The duo eventually turned a double play one batter later, but the play highlighted a growing concern with Lombard Jr. and his mental errors. A few innings prior, he couldn't haul in a line drive that hit his glove. That extended the inning and contributed to the Yankees relinquishing their lead.
In Tuesday's win, fans got hit with another bit of oddness, as Lombard Jr. took too long on a routine play with Royce Lewis running, bitten by his lack of knowledge of the base runner. Lewis reached base on a ball he absolutely should not have been rewarded for hitting, and eventually came around to score the Twins' only run on a two-out single, cutting the deficit to 2-1 (before things ballooned).
In just 33 games, Lombard Jr. has experienced some tremendous highs and embarrassing lows. He managed to hit the Yankees’ first grand slam of the season on Sept. 9 against the Colorado Rockies. He also endured a dubious six-game streak of committing an error in the field.
Yet somewhere in the middle of all of that, he’s been a serviceable player so far in his debut season. But is that enough for the Yankees? For a team that is eying a World Series run, is Lombard Jr. good enough right now to start in the postseason? With less than two weeks left in the regular season, it’s too late to back out now. For better or for worse, Lombard. Jr. will be put to the ultimate postseason test.
The Yankees don’t need George Lombard Jr. to be elite right now
Through his first 282 1/3 innings played this season, Lombard Jr. has committed eight errors. That's about an error every four games. Over the course of a full season, that would translate to around 40 errors. That would be the most errors committed by a player in a single season since José Offerman’s 42-error season in 1992. Multiplying the sample size like that isn't how things work, but there's a picture painted for you.
In a postseason series, one error could be the difference between going home or moving on. For a rookie already under increased scrutiny, Lombard Jr. could be approaching a perfect error storm. However, things may not be all doom and gloom. Lombard Jr. has not played nearly as bad as his stat sheet would appear to indicate.
With eight Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) in his limited time, Lombard Jr. already ranks in the top 10 in all of baseball among shortstops. While his Outs Above Average (1) paints a different picture, there's no reason to believe a young player with the athletic skills of Lombard Jr. won't be able to improve his range and overall reaction time. As mentioned before, it appears as if the game is moving just a little too fast at times for the rookie.
The same could be said about his approach at the plate. With a .677 OPS in August, Lombard Jr. didn't exactly set the world ablaze offensively, but he flashed his ability to go the other way and put up some very decent at-bats. His September has been a different story. Outside of his grand slam on Sept. 9, he has struggled mightily adjusting to Major League pitching.
Other teams now know his weaknesses and they have been exploiting them routinely. But with the return of Aaron Judge in the lineup, some pressure may be taken off of Lombard Jr. to give him a moment to breathe and slow down the game. Since Judge rejoined the Yankees on Sept. 8, the team is 5-1. They’ve also averaged 4.83 runs scored per game in that stretch, a bump up from their season average of 4.57. With a deeper lineup that is able to score more runs, Lombard Jr. could take advantage and make those crucial adjustments and find his swing.
Throwing a rookie into the postseason fire isn't an optimal solution, but Lombard Jr. doesn't have to be the guy to carry the team. He doesn't even need to be elite just yet. If he's able to clean up his mistakes and get back to what made him the team's top prospect, he can play a pivotal role in winning a championship for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Los Yankees han resuelto la gran incógnita de septiembre. Vuelven a octubre.
Ahora, el entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, tiene otra decisión que se vuelve cada vez más urgente: ¿quién debería jugar en tercera base cuando empiece la postemporada?
Durante casi toda la temporada, Ryan McMahon parecía la respuesta más obvia. Era el tercera base titular y un defensor de probada eficacia.
Pero la plantilla de Nueva York ha cambiado a su alrededor, lo que da a los Yankees más de una opción para formar el cuadro interior, ahora que cada turno al bate y cada entrada defensiva de la postemporada tienen más importancia.
Los Yankees también cuentan con una opción más rápida y versátil para el cuadro, capaz de cubrir varias posiciones sin obligar a Boone a recurrir a una estructura de platooning demasiado limitada. Una posición que parecía decidida se ha convertido en una auténtica incógnita de cara a la postemporada.
La alineación del martes ha cambiado el debate sobre la tercera base
McMahon estaba en el banquillo de los Yankees el martes. José Caballero fue titular en tercera base una noche después de que su actuación, con dos hits y dos carreras impulsadas, ayudara a Nueva York a asegurarse el título.
Lo más revelador es que Minnesota alineó al lanzador diestro Bailey Ober. McMahon, un bateador zurdo, había vuelto a ser titular en la tercera base en la mayoría de los partidos contra lanzadores diestros tras recuperarse de un esguince de grado 2 en el pulgar izquierdo el 1 de septiembre. Por eso, la titularidad de Caballero fue algo más que una simple decisión de rotación.
No supone un cambio permanente, pero hace que la comparación sea difícil de ignorar.
Hasta el martes, Caballero ha jugado 127 partidos y tiene un promedio de bateo de .235/.292/.376, con 14 jonrones, 49 carreras impulsadas y 32 bases robadas en 429 turnos al bate. McMahon ha jugado 117 partidos y tiene un promedio de bateo de .214/.280/.353, con 10 jonrones, 34 carreras impulsadas y tres bases robadas en 340 turnos al bate.
La comparación de Stathead que se ofrece muestra a Caballero con un WAR de 2,3 frente al 0,2 de McMahon. Caballero también tiene un OPS+ de 85 frente al 75 de McMahon.
La diferencia en ataque no es enorme, pero Caballero lidera todas las categorías estadísticas mencionadas y, además, suma cuatro jonrones más, 15 carreras impulsadas más y 29 bases robadas más. En octubre, esa velocidad extra puede ser importante, incluso cuando no se espera que ninguno de los dos jugadores sea el pilar de la alineación.
Caballero no dejaba de abrirse paso en la alineación
Cuando Caballero volvió de la lista de lesionados en mayo, Boone dijo que tanto él como Anthony Volpe se habían ganado minutos de juego y que los Yankees tendrían que hacer algunos cambios para dárselos.
Boone describió la competencia como una ventaja más que como un problema.
«Es una buena situación», dijo Boone, «porque tenemos dos jugadores que creemos que pueden desempeñar un papel clave para que ganemos los partidos».
Desde entonces, la alineación ha cambiado varias veces. La lesión en el pulgar de Jazz Chisholm Jr. hizo que Caballero pasara a jugar de segunda base la semana pasada. George Lombard Jr. y Volpe se han encargado de la posición de campo corto. Caballero ha seguido jugando dondequiera que Boone lo haya necesitado.
Esa flexibilidad ha dado lugar ahora a una duda mucho mayor de cara a octubre.
McMahon aporta experiencia y un largo historial defensivo. Caballero aporta velocidad, versatilidad defensiva y la capacidad de cubrir la segunda base, el campo corto y la tercera base sin obligar a Boone a limitarse a un papel de platoon.
El caso de Caballero va más allá del guante
El historial defensivo de McMahon hace que esto no sea una simple comparación ofensiva. Baseball-Reference le atribuye 69 «Defensive Runs Saved» (DRS) a lo largo de su carrera en tercera base. Esta temporada, sin embargo, tiene un DRS de -1 en 825 1/3 entradas jugadas en esa posición.
Caballero no tiene el volumen de partidos de McMahon en esa posición, pero su historial defensivo habla por sí solo.
A lo largo de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas en las tres posiciones del cuadro, Caballero ha registrado un DRS de +10 y un Fielding Run Value de +7 en segunda base en 903 entradas, un DRS de +5 y un FRV de +4 en tercera base en 568 1/3 entradas, y un DRS de +17 con un FRV de +10 en el campo corto en 1.763 2/3 entradas.
Por eso su caso es diferente al de un suplente que se pone en racha en el momento adecuado. Los Yankees pueden poner a Caballero en tercera sin renunciar a esa versatilidad defensiva que ya lo hace útil en otras posiciones.
Su juego en las bases aumenta la ventaja. Las 32 bases robadas de Caballero le dan a Boone un arma para los momentos decisivos del partido sin que tenga que reservar a Caballero exclusivamente para entrar como corredor suplente. Si sale de titular, esa velocidad ya está en el campo.
Además, al bate, es mejor que McMahon. Hasta el 15 de septiembre, tiene un promedio de bateo de .235/.292/.376, con 14 jonrones, 49 carreras impulsadas, 32 bases robadas y un OPS de .668. McMahon se queda en un promedio de bateo de .214/.280/.353, con 10 jonrones, 34 carreras impulsadas, tres bases robadas y un OPS de .633. Caballero también tiene un WAR de 2,3, frente al 0,2 de McMahon, lo que aporta a los Yankees más producción ofensiva, velocidad y valor general sin sacrificar la flexibilidad posicional.
Ninguno de los dos ha sido un bateador por encima de la media, pero esa diferencia cuenta ahora que Boone está decidiendo su alineación para octubre. La ventaja de Caballero ya no se basa solo en su versatilidad. Simplemente ha rendido más al bate esta temporada.
Ahora hay una diferencia de 2,1 WAR que se decidirá en octubre
La diferencia más clara en general es la de 2,1 victorias en WAR.
Caballero ha sumado 2,3 WAR en 429 turnos al bate. McMahon ha sumado 0,2 en 340. A Caballero solo le han hecho falta 89 turnos al bate más para crear esa diferencia.
McMahon sigue aportando ventajas reales. Cuenta con un amplio historial defensivo en tercera base, tiene contrato hasta 2027 y puede dar un giro a la situación con un buen final de temporada. Además, hace solo dos semanas que volvió tras la lesión en el pulgar, lo que da a los Yankees motivos para tener en cuenta las dificultades recientes.
Pero los puestos en la postemporada no se otorgan en función del tipo de contrato ni de cómo se te haya utilizado antes. Nueva York ya se ha clasificado, lo que convierte el calendario que queda en una lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, en una prueba de fuego de cara a octubre.
El lunes quedó claro que Caballero puede cambiar el rumbo de un partido con su bate y sus piernas. El martes se vio que Boone está dispuesto a alinearlo directamente en la posición de McMahon, incluso contra un lanzador diestro.
Nada garantiza que esa configuración se mantenga en octubre. Los Yankees aún tienen tiempo para probarla.
Lo que sí ha cambiado es la carga de la prueba. Caballero ya no parece un jugador polivalente al que los Yankees tienen que meter a la fuerza en un partido de postemporada. Parece un jugador capaz de ganarse un puesto en la alineación titular.
Si esto sigue así, puede que sea el papel de McMahon en octubre el que tenga que reducirse.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

That's what he is doing now, he's supporting Gary Sanchez, Miguel Andujar and last but not least Anthony Volpe, read more HERE. These guys were given "labels" from the fan base, which happens a lot when you don't meet expectations underneath New York's bright lights. For years we have been writing about how the Yankees coddle their players and but now CC wants the Yankees to also help them adapt to this demanding environment.
I agree with that to a point. New York is a tough place to play for established veterans, let alone when you are a young kid like Volpe was making it onto the big stage as an everyday player. There should be some mental preparation there for players, but it should also be prepared with the confidence of pairing that with good fundamentals to help you perform at a high level under those bright lights. If you have that track record of faltering (like Volpe has) that's when the Yankees need to be more hands on. It's exactly what the Yankees haven't done well.
Everyone in life needs feedback. It's what helps us improve and hone in on our craft. The Yankees do need to look for new ways to help guys deal with the pressures in the bright lights but maybe that doesn't look like what CC is suggesting. Maybe it's a more real-world scenario that the rest of us deal with since we don't make the big bucks playing a kid's game for a living.
The Yankees coddle; I call it the Aaron Boone approach. He's warm and fuzzy. The Bronx, however, is not a warm and fuzzy place. It's as real as it gets. Why aren't we giving that fair, but realistic approach to these guys? This isn't a sunshine and rainbows environment. This isn't a "safe space." This is a 'pull your big boy pants up and be tough' environment and get the job done. Figure it out and use your resources. The Yankees have lots of resources and patience. The fans don't have the patience, and we shouldn't be expected to have patience.
You can still give honest feedback that is firm but fair. It builds character. Hugs are not included on the side here. That's what Boone and the Yankees do. They give hugs, but they don't give reality. Give these guys a real environment to adapt in and help them through the bumps and they will perform better, period. If they don't, then they get sent down to the minors like Volpe did or traded. 
Only the strong survive here, and the Yankees need to figure that out. The coddling isn't working. Not everyone is cut out to play here so it's time to be honest about that.
